Eyelid Disorders: Management  
and Treatment  
Concise clinical guidance for initial pharmacy assessment, general management, dry-eye  
pathways, and red flags for referral.  
What Are Eyelid Disorders?  
Eyelid disorders are conditions that affect the structure, function or appearance of the eyelids. They arise from infections, gland blockages, allergic  
reactions, chronic skin disease, poor hygiene or environmental irritants.  
Bacterial infections  
Gland blockage  
Allergic & skin disease  
Commonly Staphylococcus causing  
local inflammation and discharge.  
Meibomian gland obstruction  
leads to chalazia and chronic lid  
disease.  
Allergies, seborrhoeic dermatitis or  
rosacea can inflame lids  
chronically.  
Risk Factors  
Recognise factors that predispose patients to eyelid disorders so you can advise  
prevention and identify higher-risk presentations.  
Poor hygiene  
Infrequent or improper lid cleaning increases infection risk.  
Contaminated cosmetics  
Old/contaminated makeup and sharing products spread microbes.  
Contact lens misuse  
Poor handling or overnight wear raises irritation and infection risk.  
Systemic factors  
Diabetes and immunosuppression increase susceptibility and severity.  
Common Symptoms  
Symptoms vary from mild irritation to vision impact. Use this checklist when assessing  
presentation and urgency.  
Local signs  
Redness, swelling, lump (painful or painless), crusting at lid margins.  
Sensory symptoms  
Itching, foreign-body sensation, pain or tenderness, excessive tearing or dryness.  
Visual effects  
Blurred or fluctuating vision in severe cases — treat as potential red flag.  
Pharmacy Approach — Initial  
Assessment  
Structured assessment helps decide whether to manage in pharmacy or refer urgently.  
Take a focused history, observe the lid and decide based on severity and vision  
involvement.

Eyelid Disorders)  
Core self-care and precautionary measures applicable to most eyelid disorders.  
Emphasise simplicity, repetition and safety.

Precautions  
Do not share towels or cosmetics; replace old makeup regularly; never squeeze  
lesions.

Dry-Eye Pathways — Causes  
Dry eye results from tear film instability, low tear quantity or poor tear quality. Grouping causes helps target treatment.  
Choose treatments that address the dominant pathway—lubrication, MGD therapy or anti-inflammatory measures.  
Diagnosing Dry Eye — Practical  
Steps  
Use symptom checklist and simple observations in pharmacy to identify likely dry eye  
and its drivers.  
Symptom checklist  
Burning, stinging, grittiness, foreign-body sensation  
Redness, fluctuating/worse vision with screens, tearing  
Morning symptoms, lid crusting, contact lens discomfort  
•
•
•
Observation  
Look for blepharitis/MGD: red lid margins, inspissated meibum, lash crusting and  
signs of rubbing.  
When to Refer — Red Flags  
Immediate referral is required if any red flags are present. For borderline cases, advise prompt GP or ophthalmology review  
within days.  
Vision changes  
Any new or worsening visual disturbance requires urgent assessment.  
Severe pain  
May indicate deeper infection or corneal involvement — refer immediately.  
Spreading redness  
Suggests cellulitis or severe infection — urgent referral.  
No improvement / recurrence  
No response after 3–5 days or recurrent disease and large persistent chalazion merit referral.  
If in doubt, err on the side of referral — vision and ocular health can be rapidly compromised.
